48 revs−1
24 revs−1
why: ε=NBA/(T/4)=4NBAf, so f=ε/(4NBA)=12 revolutions per second.

prompt: A generator coil of 200 turns and area 0.030 m2 turns at 25 revolutions per second in a 0.60 T field. What is the average emf induced during the quarter turn from the plane being perpendicular to the field to the plane being parallel to it?
options: 1.8×102 V
1.8 V
90 V
3.6×102 V
why: A quarter turn takes T/4=0.010 s and the flux falls by BA: ε=NBA/(T/4)=3.6×102 V.

prompt: The coil of an AC generator turns at 1800 revolutions per minute. What is the frequency of the alternating emf it produces?
options: 30 Hz
1.9×102 Hz
60 Hz
1.8×103 Hz
why: One cycle of emf is produced per revolution: 1800/60=30 revolutions per second, so 30 Hz.

prompt: The rotation speed of an AC generator is tripled. The peak emf and the frequency of the output
options: both stay the same
peak emf triples, frequency stays the same
both triple
frequency triples, peak emf stays the same
why: Turning faster changes the flux faster (larger emf) and completes more cycles per second (higher frequency).

prompt: A generator coil of 300 turns and area 0.025 m2 turns in a 0.25 T field. How many revolutions per second are needed for an average emf of 24 V over each quarter turn?
options: 13 revs−1
3.2 revs−1
9.6×102 revs−1
6.4 revs−1
why: ε=NBA/(T/4)=4NBAf, so f=ε/(4NBA)=3.2 revolutions per second.

prompt: The emf induced in a rotating generator coil is greatest when
options: the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, where the flux is maximum
the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, where the flux is zero but changing fastest
the coil is at 45° to the field
the coil is stationary
why: emf depends on the rate of change of flux, which is greatest as the coil sides cut straight across the field lines.

prompt: The emf of an AC generator is zero at the instant when
options: the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
the flux through the coil is zero
the coil sides move at right angles to the field
the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
why: At that instant the coil sides move parallel to the field lines, so the flux is momentarily not changing.

prompt: In a DC generator, the split-ring commutator
options: increases the size of the emf
keeps the coil connected to the same terminal so the output alternates
stops sparking by removing the brushes
reverses the connections to the external circuit every half turn so the output does not change direction
why: Swapping the connections each half turn, just as the coil emf reverses, keeps the output current in one direction.

prompt: The output of a simple single-coil DC generator, plotted against time, is
options: a sine wave that changes sign every half turn
a series of humps that rise and fall but never change sign
a square wave
a constant horizontal line
why: The commutator flips the negative halves of the sine wave, giving a pulsating (rectified) output.

prompt: A generator is connected to a lamp. When the lamp is switched on, the generator becomes harder to turn because
options: the coil's resistance increases
the magnetic field becomes stronger
the induced current in the coil experiences a force opposing the rotation
friction in the bearings increases
why: By Lenz's law the current produces a motor-effect torque opposing the motion, so more work is needed: mechanical energy becomes electrical.

prompt: Large power-station generators rotate an electromagnet inside fixed coils, rather than rotating the coils. A key reason is that
options: magnets cannot be held still
rotating coils cannot induce an emf
the large output current can be taken from fixed coils without sliding contacts
it produces DC instead of AC
why: Only the small field current passes through slip rings; the large output comes from the stationary windings.

prompt: Which change would NOT increase the peak emf of an AC generator?
options: Turning the coil faster
Adding more turns to the coil
Using thicker wire with the same number of turns
Using a stronger magnetic field
why: The emf depends on N, B, A and the rotation rate; wire thickness only changes resistance.

prompt: A motor and a generator are similar in structure. The main difference is that a generator
options: converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
has no magnetic field
has no coil
converts electrical energy into mechanical energy
why: A motor uses a current to make motion; a generator uses motion to induce a current.

prompt: For a generator coil, the graph of flux through the coil against time is a cosine curve. The graph of induced emf against time is
options: a straight line increasing with time
a cosine curve in step with the flux
a horizontal line
a sine curve, a quarter of a cycle out of step with the flux
why: emf is proportional to the (negative) gradient of the flux-time graph: largest where flux crosses zero, zero where flux peaks.

prompt: Brushes in a generator are made of graphite (carbon) mainly because graphite
options: conducts electricity and is slippery, so it rubs against the rings with little friction and wear
increases the induced emf
is an insulator
is a magnetic material
why: Brushes must conduct while sliding against the rotating rings.

prompt: AC generators are used for the electricity grid rather than DC generators, mainly because
options: AC has no transmission losses
AC can be stepped up and down with transformers for efficient transmission
DC cannot be produced by rotating coils
AC generators produce more energy from the same input
why: Transformers need changing flux, so they only work with AC; high-voltage transmission greatly cuts losses.

prompt: A simple AC generator has slip rings. Each slip ring
options: stays connected to the same end of the coil, so the output reverses every half turn
is a permanent magnet
swaps the connections every half turn
turns the AC into DC
why: Each ring is fixed to one end of the coil, so the external current reverses as the coil emf does.

prompt: A generator's output frequency is 50 Hz. The time for one revolution of its (single) coil is
why: One revolution gives one cycle, so T=1/f=1/50=0.020 s.

prompt: In an AC induction motor, the stator produces
options: a rotating magnetic field
a static electric field
a constant magnetic field
a direct current in the rotor through brushes
why: AC in the stator windings, arranged around the motor, creates a magnetic field that rotates.

prompt: The rotor of a common AC induction motor is called a squirrel cage because it consists of
options: permanent magnets arranged in a ring
a hollow iron drum with no conductors
conducting bars joined at each end by rings
a coil connected to slip rings
why: The bars and end rings form closed loops in which currents are induced.

prompt: Current flows in the rotor of an AC induction motor because
options: the rotating field causes a changing flux through the rotor loops, inducing currents
it is connected to the supply by brushes
the stator and rotor touch
the rotor is a permanent magnet
why: There is no electrical connection to the rotor: currents are induced by electromagnetic induction.

prompt: The rotor of an AC induction motor turns
options: in the opposite direction to the rotating field
faster than the rotating field
in the same direction as the rotating field, but slightly slower
at exactly the same speed as the rotating field
why: The induced currents oppose the relative motion, dragging the rotor after the field; it must lag behind for currents to be induced.

prompt: If the rotor of an induction motor turned at exactly the same speed as the rotating magnetic field,
options: the motor would act as a DC motor
the torque would be at its maximum
there would be no change in flux through it, so no current and no torque
the rotor would overheat
why: With no relative motion, the flux through the rotor loops is constant and nothing is induced.

prompt: An advantage of AC induction motors over DC motors with brushes is that they
options: run on DC as well as AC
need no magnetic field
always rotate at exactly the supply frequency
have no brushes or commutator to wear out or spark
why: With no sliding contacts they are reliable, need little maintenance and are safe where sparks would be dangerous.

prompt: When a heavier load is put on an induction motor, its rotor slows a little. This causes
options: the field to rotate in reverse
smaller induced currents and less torque
no change in the induced current
a greater rate of change of flux, larger induced currents and a larger torque
why: Greater slip between field and rotor means faster relative motion, inducing more current and more torque to match the load.

prompt: The iron core of an induction motor's rotor is laminated in order to
options: increase the eddy currents
reduce energy lost to eddy currents in the iron
stop current flowing in the bars
make the rotor lighter so it spins faster than the field
why: Thin insulated sheets break up eddy current paths in the core, while the bars still carry the useful currents.

prompt: The operating principle of an AC induction motor relies on
options: both electromagnetic induction and the motor effect
the motor effect only, with current supplied by brushes
electrostatic attraction
permanent magnets in the rotor
why: Induction creates the rotor currents, and the motor effect produces forces on those currents in the field.

prompt: A typical use of an AC induction motor is
options: a washing machine, pump or industrial fan
a solar panel
a quartz watch
a battery-powered toy car
why: Induction motors run from mains AC and are rugged, cheap and reliable for household and industrial machines.

prompt: The rotating magnetic field in a three-phase induction motor is produced by
options: the rotor bars
three sets of stator coils, spaced around the stator, carrying AC currents that peak one after another
a split-ring commutator
a permanent magnet spun by a separate motor
why: Currents peaking in sequence in coils spaced around the stator make the resultant field rotate.

prompt: Compared with a DC motor, the rotor of an AC induction motor
options: receives current through slip rings and brushes
receives current through a split-ring commutator
is a permanent magnet
receives no current from an external connection
why: All rotor current is induced; there are no external connections.

prompt: Which statement about the squirrel-cage rotor bars is correct?
options: They are insulated so no current flows in them
They create the rotating field
They carry induced currents and experience forces because they are in the stator's magnetic field
They are connected directly to the mains
why: Induced current in a bar inside the field gives a motor-effect force, F=lIB, which turns the rotor.

prompt: If a squirrel-cage rotor is held still while the stator is switched on, the induced rotor currents are
options: the same as at full speed
zero, because the rotor is not moving
smaller than at full speed
at their largest, because the relative motion of the field and rotor is greatest
why: The field sweeps past a stationary rotor fastest, giving the greatest rate of change of flux; this is why starting currents are large.

prompt: The direction of rotation of a three-phase induction motor can be reversed by
options: reversing the rotor bars
removing the end rings
swapping two of the three supply connections, which reverses the rotating field
adding a commutator
why: The rotor follows the field, so reversing the field's rotation reverses the motor.

prompt: Lenz's law explains why the rotor of an induction motor follows the rotating field because
options: the rotor is attracted to the brushes
the induced currents act to reduce the relative motion between the rotor and the field
the induced currents act to increase the relative motion
the rotor carries a constant current
why: Opposing the change means opposing the relative motion, so the rotor is dragged along with the field.

prompt: A simple demonstration of the induction motor principle is a metal can on a pivot near a rotating magnet. The can
options: rotates in the same direction as the magnet, more slowly
rotates the opposite way to the magnet
stays still, as it is not magnetic
rotates faster than the magnet
why: Eddy currents induced in the can oppose the relative motion, so the can is dragged around after the magnet.

prompt: In an AC induction motor, energy is transferred from the stator to the rotor by
options: a changing magnetic field (electromagnetic induction)
heat conduction
direct physical contact
brushes and slip rings
why: The rotor is electrically isolated; energy crosses the air gap through the changing magnetic field, like a transformer.

prompt: An induction motor is sometimes described as a transformer with a rotating secondary. The rotor plays the role of the
options: iron core only
primary coil, connected to the supply
secondary coil, in which currents are induced
power supply
why: The stator (primary) is supplied with AC; the rotor (secondary) carries induced currents.

prompt: A disadvantage of a simple AC induction motor compared with a DC motor is that
options: it produces sparks
its speed is hard to vary, as it is set mostly by the supply frequency
it cannot run from mains AC
it needs brushes replaced often
why: The rotor speed stays close to the field speed, fixed by supply frequency, unless a variable frequency drive is used.

prompt: The slip of an induction motor is the difference between
options: the stator current and rotor current
the rotor speed and zero
the speed of the rotating field and the speed of the rotor
the supply voltage and the back emf
why: Slip is how far the rotor lags the field; without slip there is no induced current.

prompt: Eddy current brakes slow a 6.0×104 kg train from 35 ms−1 to 5.0 ms−1 on level track. Ignoring other losses, how much energy is converted to heat in the rails and brakes?
options: 7.2×107 J
2.7×107 J
3.6×107 J
3.7×107 J
why: The kinetic energy lost is 21​m(v12​−v22​)=3.6×107 J, dissipated as heat by the eddy currents.

prompt: A magnetic brake stops a 8.0×102 kg vehicle from 12 ms−1 in 4.0 s. What is the average rate at which the eddy currents produce heat?
options: 2.9×104 W
2.3×105 W
2.4×103 W
1.4×104 W
why: Power = energy/time = 21​mv2/t=1.4×104 W.

prompt: Eddy current brakes slow a 2.5×104 kg train from 30 ms−1 to 10 ms−1 on level track. Ignoring other losses, how much energy is converted to heat in the rails and brakes?
options: 5.0×106 J
2.0×107 J
1.1×107 J
1.0×107 J
why: The kinetic energy lost is 21​m(v12​−v22​)=1.0×107 J, dissipated as heat by the eddy currents.

prompt: A magnetic brake stops a 1.5×103 kg vehicle from 12 ms−1 in 12 s. What is the average rate at which the eddy currents produce heat?
options: 1.5×103 W
9.0×103 W
1.3×106 W
1.8×104 W
why: Power = energy/time = 21​mv2/t=9.0×103 W.

prompt: In a magnetic (eddy current) brake, the braking force
options: is constant at all speeds
is greatest when the object is at rest
is greatest at high speed and becomes very small as the object nears rest
holds the object stationary once it stops
why: The induced emf, and so the eddy currents and force, depend on the rate of change of flux, which falls as speed falls.

prompt: An advantage of magnetic braking over friction braking is that
options: there is no contact, so there is no wear on brake pads
it can hold a vehicle stationary on a hill
it works better at low speed
it does not produce heat
why: No rubbing surfaces wear out; but magnetic brakes cannot hold a vehicle at rest, so friction brakes are still needed.

prompt: A copper plate swings as a pendulum between the poles of a strong magnet and quickly stops. With many slots cut into the plate it
options: swings for much longer, because the slots break up the eddy current paths
is attracted and sticks to the magnet
stops even faster
swings exactly as before
why: Slots stop large eddy current loops forming, so the opposing force is much smaller.

prompt: The energy of a vehicle slowed by eddy current brakes ends up mostly as
options: chemical energy in the battery
sound
magnetic energy stored in the magnets
heat in the conductor carrying the eddy currents
why: The eddy currents heat the conductor (I2R), dissipating the kinetic energy.

prompt: An induction cooktop heats a steel saucepan by
options: a hot element under the glass conducting heat into the pan
the motor effect pushing on the pan
microwaves absorbed by the food
a rapidly changing magnetic field inducing eddy currents in the pan base, which heat it
why: High-frequency AC in a coil under the glass creates a changing flux in the pan; the induced currents heat the pan itself.

prompt: A glass pot does not heat up on an induction cooktop because
options: glass reflects magnetic fields
the cooktop only works with water
glass is not a conductor, so no eddy currents can be induced in it
glass is too heavy
why: Induction heating needs a conducting (preferably ferromagnetic) material for eddy currents to flow.

prompt: Some roller coasters use rows of magnets on the track and copper fins on the cars to brake. When the car passes the magnets,
options: eddy currents in the fins create forces that oppose the car's motion
the magnets attract the copper and pull it to a stop
a current from the track motor slows the car
the fins become permanent magnets
why: Moving the conducting fins through the field changes the flux in them; the induced eddy currents oppose the relative motion (Lenz).

prompt: Magnetic braking is a direct application of Lenz's law because
options: the induced currents create forces that oppose the motion causing them
the induced currents add to the motion
magnets attract all metals
the brakes use friction between magnets and rails
why: Any relative motion that changes flux induces currents that oppose it.

prompt: A strong magnet slides down a sloping aluminium sheet much more slowly than down a sloping wooden board. This is because
options: the wood is magnetic
aluminium is attracted to magnets like iron
eddy currents induced in the aluminium oppose the magnet's motion
aluminium has more friction than wood
why: Aluminium is not attracted to a stationary magnet, but a moving magnet induces eddy currents that oppose its motion.

prompt: Regenerative braking in an electric car slows the car by
options: reversing the battery so the motor turns backwards
cutting all current to the motor
using the motor as a generator, so the induced current's opposing force slows the wheels while charging the battery
pressing pads onto the discs
why: Driven by the wheels, the motor generates current; by Lenz's law this produces a torque opposing the rotation, recovering energy.

prompt: A metal detector at an airport works because
options: metal objects block light beams
a changing magnetic field induces eddy currents in metal objects, whose own fields are detected
metal objects emit radioactivity
metals are attracted to the detector
why: The eddy currents in the metal produce a magnetic field that changes the signal in the detector coil.

prompt: Why can't magnetic brakes alone hold a train stationary on a slope?
options: the magnets lose their magnetism at rest
eddy currents are largest at rest
When the train is not moving, there is no change in flux, so no eddy currents and no braking force
friction cancels the magnetic force
why: Eddy current forces need relative motion; at rest they vanish.

prompt: A magnet is dropped down a vertical copper pipe. After a short time it
options: stops and stays still inside the pipe
falls at a constant, slow terminal velocity
keeps accelerating at 9.8 m s−2
speeds up then bounces back up
why: The opposing eddy current force grows with speed until it equals the magnet's weight, so the magnet stops accelerating.

prompt: An electricity meter disc or a car speedometer that uses a spinning magnet near a metal cup relies on
options: the photoelectric effect
electrostatic attraction
friction between magnet and cup
eddy currents creating a drag force proportional to the rotation speed
why: The faster the magnet spins, the larger the eddy currents and the drag on the cup, which is balanced by a spring to give the reading.

prompt: Eddy current brakes on a train are made more effective by
options: increasing the gap between magnet and rail
using stronger electromagnets
using a less conductive rail material
cutting slots in the rails
why: A stronger field gives a larger rate of change of flux, larger eddy currents and a larger opposing force.

prompt: Which of these does NOT rely on Lenz's law and eddy currents?
options: A swinging copper pendulum stopping between magnet poles
A torch with a filament bulb running from a battery
An induction cooktop
An eddy current brake on a roller coaster
why: The other three all depend on induced currents opposing a change; a battery torch has a steady current and no changing flux.

prompt: In a magnetic braking system, increasing the speed of the moving conductor
options: has no effect on the braking force
decreases the braking force
increases the braking force
reverses the braking force
why: Faster motion means a faster change of flux, larger eddy currents and a larger opposing force.

prompt: At one instant, an electromagnetic wave travelling to the left has its electric field pointing out of the page. Given that the direction of travel is the direction of E×B, what is the direction of the magnetic field at that instant?
options: towards the top of the page
out of the page
towards the bottom of the page
to the left
why: B must be perpendicular to both E and the direction of travel, and E×B must point to the left, so B points towards the top of the page.

prompt: At one instant, an electromagnetic wave travelling into the page has its electric field pointing towards the bottom of the page. Given that the direction of travel is the direction of E×B, what is the direction of the magnetic field at that instant?
options: to the left
to the right
towards the bottom of the page
into the page
why: B must be perpendicular to both E and the direction of travel, and E×B must point into the page, so B points to the left.

prompt: At one instant, an electromagnetic wave travelling to the right has its electric field pointing into the page. Given that the direction of travel is the direction of E×B, what is the direction of the magnetic field at that instant?
options: towards the bottom of the page
towards the top of the page
to the right
into the page
why: B must be perpendicular to both E and the direction of travel, and E×B must point to the right, so B points towards the top of the page.

prompt: At one instant, an electromagnetic wave travelling into the page has its electric field pointing towards the top of the page. Given that the direction of travel is the direction of E×B, what is the direction of the magnetic field at that instant?
options: to the left
into the page
to the right
towards the top of the page
why: B must be perpendicular to both E and the direction of travel, and E×B must point into the page, so B points to the right.

prompt: Maxwell calculated the speed of electromagnetic waves using
options: the charge and mass of the electron
the time light takes to cross Earth's orbit
the frequency and wavelength of visible light
the permittivity and permeability of free space, v=1/μ0​ε0​​
why: His equations gave a wave speed set entirely by the electric and magnetic constants.

prompt: Using μ0​=4π×10−7 TmA−1 and ε0​=8.854×10−12 C2N−1m−2, the speed predicted by 1/μ0​ε0​​ is
options: 2.65×10−3 ms−1
3.34×10−9 ms−1
3.00×108 ms−1
8.99×1016 ms−1
why: 1/4π×10−7×8.854×10−12​=3.00×108 ms−1, matching the measured speed of light.

prompt: The significance of Maxwell's calculated wave speed was that
options: it matched the measured speed of light, suggesting light is an electromagnetic wave
it was much faster than light, so light could not be electromagnetic
it proved light needs a medium
it showed that electricity and magnetism are unrelated
why: The agreement linked optics with electricity and magnetism.

prompt: According to Maxwell, a changing electric field
options: produces an electric current in a vacuum
has no effect on magnetic fields
produces a gravitational field
produces a magnetic field
why: This, with Faraday's law (a changing magnetic field produces an electric field), lets the two fields sustain each other as a wave.

prompt: Electromagnetic waves are produced by
options: stationary magnets
accelerating (for example, oscillating) electric charges
charges moving at constant velocity
stationary charges
why: An oscillating charge produces changing electric and magnetic fields that propagate outward.

prompt: Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum because
options: space is filled with the aether
they are longitudinal waves
their oscillating electric and magnetic fields regenerate each other without needing a medium
they are made of particles of matter
why: Each changing field induces the other, so no medium is needed.

prompt: Electromagnetic waves are
options: transverse, with electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel
longitudinal, with fields along the direction of travel
transverse, with the electric and magnetic fields parallel to each other
longitudinal pressure waves
why: Both fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of propagation and to each other.

prompt: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate
options: in phase, reaching their maximum values at the same time
in opposite directions so they cancel
a quarter of a cycle out of phase
at different frequencies
why: In a travelling EM wave the fields peak together at the same frequency.

prompt: Which list places electromagnetic waves in order of INCREASING frequency?
options: gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
radio, infrared, microwave, visible, X-ray, ultraviolet, gamma
visible, radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, gamma, X-ray
radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
why: Frequency increases (and wavelength decreases) from radio waves to gamma rays.

prompt: All of the following are true of every electromagnetic wave in a vacuum EXCEPT
options: they can all travel without a medium
they all have the same frequency
they all travel at 3.00×108 ms−1
they are all transverse
why: They share a speed and nature, but frequency (and wavelength) differs across the spectrum.

prompt: Hertz's experiments supported Maxwell's theory because the waves he produced
options: travelled at the speed of light and could be reflected, refracted and polarised like light
were longitudinal like sound
travelled much faster than light
needed a metal medium to travel
why: His radio waves behaved exactly as Maxwell's theory predicted for electromagnetic waves.

prompt: Maxwell's theory unified
options: nuclear forces and magnetism
heat and sound
gravity and electricity
electricity, magnetism and light
why: His equations showed light is an electromagnetic wave, joining optics with electromagnetism.

prompt: An antenna produces radio waves of frequency 100 MHz. The electrons in the antenna must be
options: oscillating at 3.00 MHz
moving at constant speed
stationary
oscillating at 100 MHz
why: The waves have the same frequency as the oscillating charges that produce them.

prompt: An FM radio station broadcasts at 88.5 MHz. What is the wavelength of its radio waves? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: 3.39 m
0.295 m
3.39×106 m
3.39×103 m
why: λ=c/f=3.00×108/8.85×107=3.39 m.

prompt: How long does light take to travel from the nearest star to Earth, a distance of 4.0×1016 m? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: 2.2×106 s
1.3×108 s
1.2×1025 s
7.5×10−9 s
why: t=d/c=4.0×1016/3.00×108=1.3×108 s.

prompt: Electromagnetic radiation has a frequency of 3.0×1018 Hz. What type of radiation is it? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: X-ray
infrared ray
ultraviolet ray
microwave
why: λ=c/f=1.0×10−10 m, which lies in the X-ray region.

prompt: A microwave source operates at 2.45 GHz. What is the wavelength? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: 8.17 m
1.22×108 m
0.122 m
122 m
why: λ=c/f=3.00×108/2.45×109=0.122 m.

prompt: Electromagnetic radiation has a frequency of 1.0×1010 Hz. What type of radiation is it? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: infrared ray
X-ray
ultraviolet ray
microwave
why: λ=c/f=0.030 m, which lies in the microwave region.

prompt: An FM radio station broadcasts at 104 MHz. What is the wavelength of its radio waves? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: 2.88×103 m
2.88×106 m
2.88 m
0.347 m
why: λ=c/f=3.00×108/1.04×108=2.88 m.

prompt: How long does light take to travel from the Moon to Earth, a distance of 3.8×108 m? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: 1.2×1017 s
0.021 s
0.78 s
1.3 s
why: t=d/c=3.8×108/3.00×108=1.3 s.

prompt: Electromagnetic radiation has a frequency of 3.0×1020 Hz. What type of radiation is it? (c=3.00×108 ms−1)
options: X-ray
microwave
gamma ray
infrared ray
why: λ=c/f=1.0×10−12 m, which lies in the gamma ray region.

prompt: Early measurements of the speed of light (such as Fizeau's) used light paths several kilometres long because
options: the mirrors had to be outdoors
short paths produce interference that cancels the light
light is so fast that a long path was needed for a measurable time interval
light slows down over short distances
why: Over 8 km light takes only about 5×10−5 s for the round trip, so long paths and fast rotation were needed.

prompt: Since 1983 the speed of light in a vacuum has been
options: measured more accurately every year
found to vary slightly with frequency
defined as exactly 299 792 458 m/s, with the metre defined from it
defined as exactly 3.00×108 ms−1
why: The metre is the distance light travels in 1/299 792 458 s, so c is now an exact defined constant.

prompt: If the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum is halved, its frequency
options: stays the same
halves
quadruples
doubles
why: In a vacuum c=fλ is constant, so f is inversely proportional to λ.

prompt: In Fizeau's toothed-wheel experiment, increasing the rotation speed of the wheel from zero, the returning light first disappears because
options: the light slows down
the mirror moves away
in the round-trip time, a gap has been replaced by the next tooth
the wheel produces interference
why: The light that passed through a gap returns to find a tooth blocking it, so the travel time equals the time to turn half a tooth spacing.

prompt: A spectral line with a laboratory wavelength of 656.3 nm is observed in a star's spectrum at 661.1 nm. The star is moving
options: away from Earth at 4.1×107 ms−1
towards Earth at 2.2×106 ms−1
away from Earth at 7.3×10−3 ms−1
away from Earth at 2.2×106 ms−1
why: Red shift: v=cΔλ/λ=3.00×108×4.8/656.3=2.2×106 ms−1 away from Earth.

prompt: A galaxy moves away from Earth at 6.0×104 ms−1. By how much is a line of laboratory wavelength 486.1 nm shifted, and in which direction?
options: 0.12 nm towards longer wavelengths

options: They have the same range, but the 60° projectile stays in the air longer
The 30° projectile has the greater range
The 60° projectile has the greater range
They have the same time of flight
why: Complementary angles give equal ranges; time of flight ∝sinθ is greater for 60°.

prompt: On a graph of vertical displacement against time for a projectile, the gradient at the highest point is
options: zero, because the vertical velocity is zero there
−9.8, the acceleration
equal to the horizontal velocity
at its greatest value
why: The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity, and vy​=0 at the top.

prompt: A student plots speed (not velocity) against time for a projectile launched at 45° from level ground. The graph
options: falls steadily until the projectile lands
is a horizontal line
falls to zero at the top, then rises
falls to a minimum equal to ux​ at the top, then rises again
why: Speed is vx2​+vy2​​, smallest when vy​=0, where it equals vx​.

prompt: In an experiment a ball is dropped from different heights h and the fall time t is measured. A graph of h (vertical axis) against t2 is a straight line with gradient 4.60 ms−2. The experimental value of g is
options: 2.14 ms−2
9.20 ms−2
2.30 ms−2
4.60 ms−2
why: h=21​gt2, so the gradient is g/2 and g=2×4.60=9.20 ms−2.

prompt: A projectile launcher is predicted to give a range of 4.10 m but the mean measured range is 3.89 m. The percentage difference from the prediction is
why: (predicted−measured)/predicted×100=(4.10−3.89)/4.10×100=5.1%.

prompt: In a lab, a ball leaves a horizontal ramp 0.80 m above the floor and lands 1.21 m from the foot of the table. Using g=9.8 ms−2, the launch speed is
options: 0.490 ms−1
4.24 ms−1
3.00 ms−1
7.42 ms−1
why: Fall time t=2h/g​=0.404 s, so u=x/t=3.00 ms−1.

prompt: In an experiment a ball is dropped from different heights h and the fall time t is measured. A graph of h (vertical axis) against t2 is a straight line with gradient 4.85 ms−2. The experimental value of g is
options: 4.85 ms−2
2.20 ms−2
2.42 ms−2
9.70 ms−2
why: h=21​gt2, so the gradient is g/2 and g=2×4.85=9.70 ms−2.

prompt: A projectile launcher is predicted to give a range of 1.95 m but the mean measured range is 1.85 m. The percentage difference from the prediction is
why: (predicted−measured)/predicted×100=(1.95−1.85)/1.95×100=5.1%.

prompt: In a lab, a ball leaves a horizontal ramp 1.0 m above the floor and lands 1.81 m from the foot of the table. Using g=9.8 ms−2, the launch speed is
options: 8.85 ms−1
0.816 ms−1
4.00 ms−1
5.66 ms−1
why: Fall time t=2h/g​=0.452 s, so u=x/t=4.00 ms−1.

prompt: In an experiment a ball is dropped from different heights h and the fall time t is measured. A graph of h (vertical axis) against t2 is a straight line with gradient 4.80 ms−2. The experimental value of g is
options: 2.40 ms−2
9.60 ms−2
2.19 ms−2
4.80 ms−2
why: h=21​gt2, so the gradient is g/2 and g=2×4.80=9.60 ms−2.

prompt: Compared with the ideal (no air resistance) path, a real projectile with air resistance has
options: the same range but a lower maximum height
a symmetrical path that is just smaller
a higher maximum height and a shorter range
a lower maximum height, a shorter range and a steeper descent than ascent
why: Drag opposes the velocity in both directions, reducing both components; the horizontal speed falls during flight, so the path is not symmetrical.

prompt: With air resistance, the launch angle that gives a projectile its greatest range on level ground is
options: exactly 45°
more than 45°
less than 45°
why: Drag reduces range most for long, high flights, so a flatter launch (below 45°) maximises range.

prompt: In a projectile investigation, which change would most improve the reliability of the range results?
options: Repeating each trial several times and averaging
Recording results to more decimal places than the ruler allows
Using a longer ruler to measure the range
Changing the launch angle each trial
why: Reliability is about consistency; repeats and averaging reduce the effect of random error.

prompt: A student always reads the launch height from above the ruler at an angle, so every height is 1 cm too high. This is
options: not an error, as it is the same each time
a random error, which affects reliability
a systematic error, which affects accuracy
a random error, which is removed by averaging
why: A consistent offset in the same direction is systematic; repeating does not remove it.

prompt: Students time the flight of a ball with a hand-held stopwatch. The main source of error is
options: air resistance, which is a random error
the mass of the ball
human reaction time, which is a random error
the value of g being wrong
why: Reaction time varies each trial (about 0.2 s), giving random error; a video or light gates reduce it.

prompt: To test whether the horizontal velocity of a projectile is constant, the best method is to
options: measure its maximum height for several angles
film it against a grid and measure horizontal distance moved in equal time intervals
measure the range for several masses
time the whole flight with a stopwatch
why: Equal horizontal distances in equal time intervals show constant vx​.

prompt: In an investigation of how launch angle affects range, which variables must be controlled?
options: Range and time of flight
Launch angle and range
Launch speed and launch height
Launch angle only
why: Angle is independent, range is dependent; speed and height must be kept constant for a valid test.

prompt: A ping pong ball and a golf ball are launched at the same speed and angle. The ping pong ball lands much shorter mainly because
options: gravity pulls harder on lighter objects
gravity does not act on light objects
its horizontal velocity increases
its small mass means air resistance gives it a much larger deceleration
why: Drag forces are similar in size, but a=F/m is much larger for the lighter ball.

prompt: A graph of range against launch angle (0° to 90°) for an ideal projectile on level ground is
options: symmetrical about 45°, with a maximum there
symmetrical about 30°
a straight line increasing with angle
greatest at 90°
why: Range ∝sin2θ, which is symmetrical about 45° on 0° to 90°.

prompt: A student wants a straight-line graph to check that range is proportional to the square of launch speed. They should plot
options: range against u
range squared against u
range against u2
range against 1/u
why: If R∝u2, plotting R against u2 gives a straight line through the origin.

prompt: The model R=u2sin2θ/g assumes that
options: there is no air resistance and launch and landing heights are equal
the projectile is launched from a height
the projectile is launched horizontally
air resistance is constant
why: The range equation is derived for level ground with gravity as the only force.

prompt: A measured range is consistently 15% below the predicted range for every trial. The most likely explanation is
options: random reaction-time error
parallax when reading the ruler, which averages out
air resistance or friction in the launcher, a systematic effect
that g is larger in the lab
why: A consistent shortfall in one direction points to a systematic cause such as drag or energy lost in the launcher.

prompt: Which change to a projectile experiment reduces the percentage uncertainty in measured range?
options: Using a smaller launch speed
Increasing the launch speed so the range is longer
Doing fewer trials
Measuring with a ruler with larger divisions
why: The same absolute uncertainty is a smaller percentage of a larger measurement.

prompt: In a Thomson-type experiment, cathode rays pass undeflected through crossed fields E=3.2×104 Vm−1 and B=2.0×10−3 T. When the electric field is switched off, the rays move in a circle of radius 0.0455 m. What is the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles?
options: 3.52×108 Ckg−1
5.69×10−12 Ckg−1
7.73×109 Ckg−1
1.76×1011 Ckg−1
why: v=E/B, and qvB=mv2/r gives q/m=v/(Br)=E/(B2r).

prompt: In a Thomson-type experiment, cathode rays pass undeflected through crossed fields E=1.5×104 Vm−1 and B=1.2×10−3 T. When the electric field is switched off, the rays move in a circle of radius 0.0590 m. What is the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles?
options: 3.59×109 Ckg−1
2.12×108 Ckg−1
5.66×10−12 Ckg−1
1.77×1011 Ckg−1
why: v=E/B, and qvB=mv2/r gives q/m=v/(Br)=E/(B2r).

prompt: In a Thomson-type experiment, cathode rays pass undeflected through crossed fields E=2.4×104 Vm−1 and B=1.5×10−3 T. When the electric field is switched off, the rays move in a circle of radius 0.0605 m. What is the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles?
options: 5.67×10−12 Ckg−1
2.64×108 Ckg−1
1.76×1011 Ckg−1
4.37×109 Ckg−1
why: v=E/B, and qvB=mv2/r gives q/m=v/(Br)=E/(B2r).

prompt: Two parallel plates 0.0200 m apart have a potential difference of 1.5×103 V. A magnetic field of 2.5×10−3 T is applied at right angles so that cathode rays pass straight through. What is the speed of the cathode rays?
options: 190 ms−1
3.0×107 ms−1
7.5×104 ms−1
1.2×104 ms−1
why: E=V/d and for no deflection qE=qvB, so v=E/B.

prompt: Two parallel plates 0.0100 m apart have a potential difference of 800 V. A magnetic field of 4.0×10−3 T is applied at right angles so that cathode rays pass straight through. What is the speed of the cathode rays?
options: 320 ms−1
2.0×107 ms−1
2.0×103 ms−1
8.0×104 ms−1
why: E=V/d and for no deflection qE=qvB, so v=E/B.

prompt: An electron in a cathode ray beam moves at 2.0×107 ms−1 at right angles to a magnetic field of 1.5×10−3 T. What is the radius of its circular path?
options: 140 m
13 m
1.1×10−4 m
0.076 m
why: qvB=mv2/r gives r=mv/(qB) using the electron mass.

prompt: An electron in a cathode ray beam moves at 5.0×106 ms−1 at right angles to a magnetic field of 4.0×10−4 T. What is the radius of its circular path?
options: 0.071 m
2.8×10−5 m
130 m
14 m
why: qvB=mv2/r gives r=mv/(qB) using the electron mass.

prompt: Electrons in a cathode ray tube are accelerated from rest through 2000 V. What speed do they reach (non-relativistic)?
options: 6.19×105 ms−1
7.03×1014 ms−1
1.88×107 ms−1
2.65×107 ms−1
why: qV=21​mv2, so v=2qV/m​.

prompt: Cathode rays are deflected towards the positive plate when they pass between charged plates. This shows that they
options: carry positive charge
carry negative charge
have no mass
are electromagnetic waves
why: Opposite charges attract.

prompt: A Maltese cross placed in a cathode ray tube casts a sharp shadow on the end of the tube. This shows that cathode rays
options: have a very small mass
are deflected by magnetic fields
travel in straight lines from the cathode
are negatively charged
why: A sharp shadow means the rays travel in straight lines from the cathode.

prompt: Cathode rays can make a small paddle wheel in the tube turn. This was taken as evidence that cathode rays
options: travel faster than light
carry positive charge
carry momentum, so they behave like particles with mass
are electromagnetic waves
why: Transferring momentum suggested particles. (Heating effects may also contribute.)

prompt: Thomson found that the charge-to-mass ratio of cathode ray particles
options: depended on the cathode metal used
was zero, since the particles were neutral
was the same for every cathode metal and gas used, and much larger than that of a hydrogen ion
was smaller than that of a hydrogen ion
why: This suggested a universal particle much lighter than any atom: the electron.

prompt: Before Thomson, many German physicists thought cathode rays were waves because
options: the rays could pass through thin metal foils, unlike any wave
early experiments did not detect any deflection by an electric field
the rays made the glass glow green
the rays were deflected by magnetic fields
why: Hertz saw no electric deflection; Thomson later succeeded with a much better vacuum.

prompt: Thomson's discovery of the electron led him to propose that the atom is
options: electrons orbiting in fixed energy levels
a solid indivisible sphere
a tiny dense positive nucleus with electrons orbiting it
a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it (the "plum pudding" model)
why: The atom is neutral overall, so the electrons must be balanced by positive charge.

prompt: In Thomson's experiment, the electric and magnetic fields are adjusted until the beam is undeflected. At this point
options: the electric force equals the magnetic force, so v=E/B
the beam has zero speed
the electric force is twice the magnetic force
both fields are zero
why: qE=qvB for no net force.

prompt: A student finds that cathode rays bend into a circle in a magnetic field. If the speed of the rays is doubled, the radius of the circle
options: increases four times
halves
stays the same
doubles
why: r=mv/(qB) is proportional to v.

prompt: An oil drop of mass 1.96×10−15 kg is held stationary between horizontal plates 10 mm apart when the potential difference is 400 V. What is the charge on the drop?
options: 7.68×10−10 C
4.80×10−15 C
7.84×10−11 C
4.80×10−19 C
why: qE=mg with E=V/d, so q=mgd/V (convert mm to m).

prompt: An oil drop of mass 2.04×10−15 kg is held stationary between horizontal plates 10 mm apart when the potential difference is 250 V. What is the charge on the drop?
options: 5.10×10−11 C
5.00×10−10 C
8.00×10−19 C
8.00×10−15 C
why: qE=mg with E=V/d, so q=mgd/V (convert mm to m).

prompt: An oil drop of mass 3.14×10−15 kg is held stationary between horizontal plates 10 mm apart when the potential difference is 320 V. What is the charge on the drop?
options: 9.62×10−15 C
9.85×10−10 C
1.00×10−10 C
9.62×10−19 C
why: qE=mg with E=V/d, so q=mgd/V (convert mm to m).

prompt: An oil drop of mass 6.81×10−16 kg is held stationary between horizontal plates 12 mm apart when the potential difference is 250 V. What is the charge on the drop?
options: 1.42×10−11 C
2.22×10−15 C
3.20×10−19 C
1.39×10−10 C
why: qE=mg with E=V/d, so q=mgd/V (convert mm to m).

prompt: An oil drop in Millikan's experiment carries a charge of 4.81×10−19 C. How many excess electrons does it carry?
why: n=q/e=4.81×10−19/1.602×10−19=3.

prompt: An oil drop in Millikan's experiment carries a charge of 8.01×10−19 C. How many excess electrons does it carry?
why: n=q/e=8.01×10−19/1.602×10−19=5.

prompt: An oil drop in Millikan's experiment carries a charge of 1.28×10−18 C. How many excess electrons does it carry?
why: n=q/e=1.28×10−18/1.602×10−19=8.

prompt: An oil drop of mass 4.9×10−15 kg carries 2 excess electrons. What potential difference across plates 12 mm apart will hold it stationary?
options: 1.8×103 V
180 V
3.6×103 V
1.2×107 V
why: qV/d=mg⇒V=mgd/q with q=ne.

prompt: An oil drop of mass 6.5×10−15 kg carries 4 excess electrons. What potential difference across plates 10 mm apart will hold it stationary?
options: 4.0×103 V
100 V
9.9×106 V
990 V
why: qV/d=mg⇒V=mgd/q with q=ne.

prompt: A student measures these charges on oil drops: 3.2, 4.8, 8.0 and 6.4×10−19 C. What is the largest charge that all of these could be whole-number multiples of?
options: 5.6×10−19 C
1.6×10−19 C
0.8×10−19 C
3.2×10−19 C
why: Each value is 2, 3, 5 or 4 times 1.6×10−19 C.

prompt: Which measured oil-drop charge is most likely to contain a large experimental error?
options: 6.4×10−19 C
9.6×10−19 C
4.8×10−19 C
5.6×10−19 C
why: 5.6/1.6=3.5, not a whole number, so it does not fit charge quantisation.

prompt: In Millikan's experiment, a drop is stationary between the plates. Which forces are balanced?
options: The magnetic force and the weight
The electric force and air resistance
The upward electric force and the downward weight
The weight and air resistance
why: Stationary means no net force: qE=mg.

prompt: The top plate is positive and a stationary oil drop is between the plates. The drop
options: is negatively charged
is positively charged
could have either sign of charge
is neutral
why: The electric force must be upward, towards the positive top plate, so the drop is negative.

prompt: While a drop is held stationary, the voltage between the plates is increased. The drop will
options: lose charge
accelerate downwards
accelerate upwards
stay stationary
why: The electric force qV/d is now greater than its weight.

prompt: Millikan used oil rather than water for his drops mainly because
options: oil drops are always positively charged
oil does not evaporate quickly, so the mass of the drop stays constant
oil is a better conductor
water drops cannot be charged
why: A changing mass would ruin the force balance.

prompt: In Millikan's experiment, X-rays or friction from the atomiser were used to
options: give the oil drops an electric charge
make the drops visible
heat the drops so they rise
measure the size of the drops
why: Ionising radiation adds or removes electrons.

prompt: Millikan found the mass of each drop by
options: measuring its charge and dividing by e
weighing it on a balance
measuring its deflection in a magnetic field
measuring its terminal velocity as it fell with the field off, and using the air resistance (Stokes' law)
why: At terminal velocity weight equals drag, which depends on the radius.

prompt: A stationary drop suddenly starts to rise, with the voltage unchanged. The most likely reason is that it
options: gained extra charge of the same sign, increasing the electric force
gained mass
became neutral
lost all of its charge
why: Picking up an extra electron (for a negative drop) increases qE.

prompt: Combining Millikan's value of e with Thomson's value of e/m allowed scientists to
options: find the speed of light
measure the radius of the nucleus
calculate the mass of the proton
calculate the mass of the electron
why: m=e/(e/m), about 9.1×10−31 kg.

prompt: In the Geiger-Marsden experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. This showed that
options: most of the atom is empty space
electrons are spread evenly through the atom
gold atoms are very small
the atom has a dense positive nucleus
why: Very few particles came close to anything that could deflect them.

prompt: A very small number of alpha particles were deflected through angles greater than 90°. Rutherford concluded that
options: the atom is mostly empty space
the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus
alpha particles have negative charge
electrons orbit in fixed energy levels
why: Only a massive, concentrated charge could repel alpha particles that strongly.

prompt: Why did the plum pudding model predict that alpha particles would pass through gold foil with only tiny deflections?
options: The positive charge was spread thinly over the whole atom, so the electric forces on an alpha particle were weak
Alpha particles have no charge
Electrons would attract the alpha particles strongly
The gold atoms were too far apart
why: Spread-out charge cannot produce a strong enough force to turn a fast alpha particle back.

prompt: Gold was used for the foil in the Geiger-Marsden experiment mainly because
options: it has no electrons
it is magnetic
it emits alpha particles
it can be hammered into a foil only a few hundred atoms thick
why: A thin foil means most alpha particles interact with at most one nucleus.

prompt: The alpha particles bounced back from the gold foil because of
options: electrostatic repulsion between the positive alpha particle and the positive nucleus
collisions with electrons
the magnetic field of the gold
gravitational attraction to the nucleus
why: Like charges repel.

prompt: Which observation from the gold foil experiment was most surprising, compared with the plum pudding model?
options: Some alpha particles were scattered back towards the source
The alpha particles were detected by flashes on a zinc sulfide screen
The foil did not melt
Most alpha particles passed straight through
why: Rutherford compared it to a shell bouncing off tissue paper.

prompt: A major problem with Rutherford's nuclear model was that, according to classical physics,
options: alpha particles should never be deflected
orbiting electrons are accelerating, so they should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
the nucleus should be negatively charged
atoms should be much larger
why: Accelerating charges emit electromagnetic radiation, so the atom would be unstable.

prompt: Rutherford's model could not explain
options: why some alpha particles bounce back
why the nucleus is positive
why atoms emit light only at particular wavelengths (line spectra)
why most alpha particles pass through foil
why: A spiralling electron would emit a continuous spectrum.

prompt: How did the gold foil experiment change the model of the atom?
options: From positive charge spread throughout the atom to a tiny dense positive nucleus with electrons around it
From a nuclear atom to the plum pudding model
From a solid sphere to a neutron-filled nucleus
From electrons in orbits to electrons in shells
why: Large-angle scattering needed a concentrated nucleus.

prompt: The fraction of alpha particles scattered through large angles was tiny. This tells us that
options: electrons are much heavier than alpha particles
alpha particles are much heavier than gold nuclei
the nucleus is negatively charged
the nucleus occupies a very small fraction of the atom's volume
why: The chance of a close approach depends on the nucleus's tiny cross-section.

prompt: In the Geiger-Marsden apparatus, the experiment was done in a vacuum because
options: the zinc sulfide screen only glows in a vacuum
alpha particles travel faster than light in a vacuum
alpha particles would be stopped by just a few centimetres of air
gold reacts with air
why: Alpha particles are highly ionising and have a short range in air.

prompt: Alpha particles are deflected only slightly by the electrons in the gold atoms because
options: electrons are inside the nucleus
electrons have far less mass than alpha particles
alpha particles are neutral
electrons have no charge
why: An alpha particle is about 7300 times as massive as an electron.

prompt: Rutherford's model is described as a "planetary" model because
options: atoms are as large as planets
electrons orbit the nucleus as planets orbit the Sun, held by electrostatic attraction
the nucleus orbits the electrons
gravity holds the electrons in place
why: The central force is electrostatic rather than gravitational.

prompt: An alpha particle heading straight for a nucleus slows down, stops and reverses. At its closest point, its kinetic energy has
options: been converted entirely into electric potential energy
doubled
been absorbed by the electrons
been converted into mass
why: The repulsive force does negative work until the alpha particle stops.

prompt: An atom has a radius of about 1.4×10−10 m and its nucleus has a radius of about 7.0×10−15 m. How many times larger is the radius of the atom than that of the nucleus?
options: 2.0×104
8.0×1012
4.0×108
5.0×10−5
why: Divide the radii; the volume ratio would be the cube of this.

prompt: An atom has a radius of about 1.0×10−10 m and its nucleus has a radius of about 5.0×10−15 m. How many times larger is the radius of the atom than that of the nucleus?
options: 2.0×104
4.0×108
5.0×10−5
8.0×1012
why: Divide the radii; the volume ratio would be the cube of this.

prompt: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 5.0 MeV travels straight towards a gold nucleus (Z=79). Using rkq1​q2​​=K, what is its distance of closest approach?
options: 2.3×10−14 m
4.6×10−14 m
4.6×10−8 m
7.3×10−27 m
why: r=Kk(2e)(Ze)​, with K converted from MeV to joules.

prompt: An alpha particle with kinetic energy 7.7 MeV travels straight towards a gold nucleus (Z=79). Using rkq1​q2​​=K, what is its distance of closest approach?
options: 1.5×10−14 m
4.7×10−27 m
3.0×10−14 m
3.0×10−8 m
why: r=Kk(2e)(Ze)​, with K converted from MeV to joules.

prompt: When beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles, a very penetrating radiation was produced that was not deflected by electric or magnetic fields. This showed the radiation was
options: made of protons
made of electrons
positively charged
electrically neutral
why: Charged particles would be deflected by the fields.

prompt: Before Chadwick's work, the penetrating radiation from beryllium was thought to be
options: high-energy gamma radiation
alpha particles
cathode rays
beta particles
why: Like gamma rays, it was neutral and very penetrating.

prompt: Chadwick placed paraffin wax in the path of the radiation from beryllium. Paraffin was chosen because
options: it is a good conductor
it is rich in hydrogen, so the radiation could knock out protons that could then be detected
it emits alpha particles
it absorbs all gamma rays
why: Protons are charged, so they are easy to detect and measure.

prompt: Chadwick rejected the idea that the beryllium radiation was gamma rays because
options: gamma photons would need far more energy (about 50 MeV) than was available to give the protons their measured energy
gamma rays cannot pass through beryllium
gamma rays are charged
gamma rays would have been deflected by the fields
why: Momentum and energy conservation made the gamma explanation impossible.

prompt: Chadwick concluded that the beryllium radiation consisted of
options: neutral particles with a mass close to that of the proton
photons with very high energy
helium nuclei
neutral particles with a mass close to that of the electron
why: A particle of similar mass can transfer most of its energy to a proton in a collision.

prompt: Which nuclear equation describes the reaction that Chadwick studied?
options: 24​He+49​Be→613​C+γ
24​He+49​Be→612​C+01​n
24​He+49​Be→612​C+11​p
01​n+49​Be→410​Be+γ
why: Mass number 13 = 12 + 1, atomic number 6 = 6 + 0.

prompt: A neutron collides head-on and elastically with a stationary proton. Since their masses are almost equal, after the collision
options: the proton stays still
the neutron almost stops and the proton moves off with nearly the neutron's original velocity
the neutron bounces back with the same speed
both move off together at half the speed
why: Equal masses in a head-on elastic collision exchange velocities.

prompt: Why was the neutron so much harder to discover than the proton and electron?
options: It is much heavier than the proton
It decays instantly
It only exists outside the nucleus
It has no charge, so it is not deflected by fields and does not ionise atoms directly
why: Detectors of the time relied on charge and ionisation.

prompt: The discovery of the neutron helped explain
options: why electrons orbit the nucleus
the photoelectric effect
why the mass of most nuclei is about twice the mass of their protons alone
why the nucleus is positive
why: Neutrons add mass but no charge.

prompt: Rutherford had predicted the existence of the neutron because
options: line spectra could not be explained
electrons were found in cathode rays
alpha particles were deflected by gold nuclei
atomic masses were larger than could be explained by the protons alone, with no extra charge
why: He proposed a neutral particle in the nucleus about a decade before Chadwick found it.

prompt: Chadwick used the conservation of which quantities to determine the mass of the neutron?
options: Angular momentum of electrons
Momentum and kinetic energy in collisions with hydrogen and nitrogen nuclei
Charge and mass number in nuclear reactions only
Electric potential energy only
why: Comparing recoil speeds of nuclei of known mass gave the neutron mass.

prompt: In a head-on elastic collision, a neutron gives a larger recoil speed to a hydrogen nucleus than to a nitrogen nucleus because
options: the neutron is attracted to hydrogen
the nitrogen nucleus is charged and the hydrogen nucleus is not
nitrogen nuclei absorb neutrons
the hydrogen nucleus has a mass close to the neutron's, so more momentum and energy are transferred
why: Recoil speed v=2mu/(m+M) falls as the target mass M rises.

prompt: Neutrons with the same speed collide head-on, elastically, with stationary hydrogen nuclei (1 u) and nitrogen nuclei (14 u). The maximum recoil speed of the hydrogen nuclei is 7.02 times that of the nitrogen nuclei. Using v=m+M2mu​, what is the neutron mass m?
options: 0.994 u
